The pattern is exactly as described. Every wrapper in ducklib.py:275-1431 repeats the C function name three times inside the wrapper block (@cres key, def name, _call_lib_func string) plus once in the signatures dict assignment block above. No test exists that asserts these three occurrences are consistent with each other or with the signatures dict key. All 190 _call_lib_func occurrences currently match their def names (verified in review notes).

The finding's claim that drift 'surfaces only as a runtime lookup failure' is partially imprecise: a typo in the @cres(signatures.get('TYPO')) decorator key returns None, and numbox/utils/highlevel.py:28-29 raises ValueError('Expected a single signature, found None') at ducklib.py import time, not at runtime. A typo in the _call_lib_func('TYPO') string surfaces as a TypingError at JIT compile time (first call) via numbox/core/bindings/call.py:73-77 (symbol not in LLVM context) or :76-77 (not in signatures dict). The only genuinely silent failure path is if the typo string matches a different DuckDB symbol that also has a matching signature registered — vanishingly unlikely in practice.

These partial guards (import-time and JIT-time errors) make the hazard slightly less acute than described, but they are not a test: they don't catch a mismatch between the decorator key and the _call_lib_func string when both happen to resolve to real, differently-named symbols. The core defect — mechanical 4x repetition with no structural test enforcing consistency — is real. The recommendation (add a test asserting each wrapper's _call_lib_func literal equals its def name and is a registered key) is sound and low-cost. Severity 'low' is correct.
